game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I'll be honest, when I purchased Orwell I did so on a steam sale, as my expectations of this game were not high. I thought that this would be the game you "play for a few hours because you bought it and it's kind of OK, and maybe you'll finish it in a few months, but in reality you never will and every-single-time you see the game in the library you'll think "Oh, better finish that!" and then feel guilty for spending the money, but at least you got it on a sale!" kind of game. 

I did not expect to be sitting at the edge of my seat every Thursday for a new episode, grieving over the things that happen to the lives I'm invading and battling with my own morals and conscience half the time. Orwell, seriously, has become one of my top 5 favorites. As devoted fan of "Life is Strange", I didn't think Orwell would emotionally capture me the same way I felt in that game, but I'd say it has. You become familiar and interested in the lives you investigate, almost personalizing them to your own life and experiences in ways I didn't think were possible. 

Now for the Tl;dr: 

Pros 
[*] Amazing storyline - keeps you interested and captivated
[*] Unique format - I've never personally played a game like this before, and the fact it's 'you' controlling the information put into the computer system makes it feel that much more personalized. You start feeling like this is your actual job. 
[*] Choice based - although some of the storyline is somewhat linear, I have heard of different outcomes for different plots 
[*] Emotionally captivating - no spoilers, but you defiitely have your heartstrings tugged at least once or twice
[*] Has replay value - I'm honestly about to start over when I finish this storyline so see how my choices effect gameplay in the end. 

Cons
[*] The game highlights sections of information that is important to your investigation, and although this is helpful, sometimes I wish that we would [b]have[/b] to read the information and it wasn't highlighted until we asked for a "hint" on what information we needed. That may be too difficult to programme, and maybe some people would hate that format/idea, but I think it would add more value in terms of gameplay. 


Overall, this game is a solid 5/5 for me!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Description[/h1]

Orwell is a visual novel that puts you in the shoes of a Big Brother employee: you are tasked with spying on people and uploading to the system anything suspicious. Unlike most visual novels, you are not presented here with walls of text followed by lists of choices. Rather, your interaction with the game and its unfolding story goes solely through the gimmick of uploading the data chunks you find (or not). By picking among conflicting data chunks or by choosing not to upload some sensitive information, you impact the story in small and big ways.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
[*] Fresh interaction gimmick that goes very well with the theme
[*] Credible writing with many characters each having their own style of speech
[*] Interesting choices going WAY beyond the good/bad dichotomy
[*] Decent art style
[*] Fair amount of consequences to choices made, though the game remains linear
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
[*] Notification system takes some getting used to ([spoiler]the system will sometimes find old information suddenly relevant, requiring you to regularly browse through the lists of documents to make sure no red star has popped[/spoiler])
[*] Because all chats and phone calls are delivered sloooooowly (and I found no way to speed them up), replaying the game to get the achievements or test other choices is a bit of a chore
[*] Political messages are (very) thinly veiled and might annoy (or even anger?) some players
[/list]

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

Do you hate it when someone tries to convey a political message artistically and ends up as subtle as a bull in a china shop? If so, stay away from this game. You're going to hate it.

Still here? OK, here's an idea: put yourself in the shoes of an orwellian enforcer and imagine the consequences of government trampling all over freedom, privacy and presumption of innocence.

Interested? Then try Orwell. Go in expecting a fresh visual novel and a politically charged (to the point of being heavy-handed at times) thought experiment. There is much to like.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Preface[/h1]
This review is being written before the conclusion of the game in episode five. I've played through the first four episodes a couple times exploring different outcomes, however, as episode five is not out yet I'm not able to comment on the totallity of the story.

[h1]The Machine[/h1]
[b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] has a very close [url=http://www.cbs.com/shows/person_of_interest/]Person of Interest[/url] vibe. The government of the fictitious country has obtained a Machine, or System, that surveils the populous gathering information however it does not act on the gathered information. The idea of the game is that the system, aptly named [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b], isn't able to decern human subtlety, sarcasim, or deciet. As such, the fictious government has [b]outsourced[/b] the task of resolving conflicts in the data, and identifying what is relevant and what is not. You as the player take on this role as an outsider to the country, tasked with sifting through the data that [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] gives you access to inorder to identify person(s) of interest. This is a role somewhat like [i]Person of Interest[/i]'s Harold Finch.

[h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is Not[/h1]
I've seen several complaints that the game isn't challenging enough, many comparing it to several "hacker simulators" such as [b][i]Hacknet[/i][/b] or [b][i]UPLINK[/i][/b]. On the surface the concept might seem somewhat similar to games such as these, however, this is not what [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] is. In this game you are not doing any "hacking" or "cracking", that is [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b]'s job. You are more of a data analyst telling a hacker, that happens to be a computer system, what data is relevant and linked to certian people. Treating it in the same vein as other "hacker simulators" isn't fair to the game and if that is what you are expecting, you will be dissapointed.

[h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is[/h1]
So if [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] isn't a "hacker simulator" what is it? I've also seen the categorization as a "visual novel" which is much closer to what this game is. The game play is reminiscent of [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choose_Your_Own_Adventure]Choose Your Own Adventure[/url] books some of you might have read as a child. As such, the outcomes that occur in the game depend on what data you choose to "flag" or "link" to someone as relevant. This process will estabilsh relationships between persons of interest that may uncover new motivations, or might change the context of the data you have available. The game is about you being the guiding hand for a surveillance system tasked with preventing & solving crime.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Interesting visual style
    [*]Enjoyable storyline that feels very linear (as it should), but leaves you with a sprinkling of "what if" moments where you feel things could have been different.
    [*]Fairly Intuitive gameplay.
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Somewhat short, although there is some replay value if you want to try to achieve different outcomes from prior play through(s)
    [*]You aren't able to link data to someone until [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] identifies it as potentially relevant.
    [*]You aren't able to revise or change "known" data based on new information
    [*]You aren't able to alter "data conflicts" if you find additional information
    [*]No "Save Game" system, uses the idea of profiles instead to allow for differing play throughs
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
The game is a fun and enjoyable experience if you do not have unrealistic expectations of what the game is and what the gameplay is like. It offers an interesting and thought provoking social commentary on the age of information technology that we live in. The game presents the idea of freedom & privacy -vs- surveillance & security in an interesting and fairly balanced way. If you actually think about what you are doing moment-by-moment in the game, you will likely find yourself re-evaluating your thoughts on these topics. That isn't to say this game is going to challenge your views or change your mind, simply that you will likely find yourself thinking about these topics and why you hold your views on these topics.

If you enjoy naritive driven experiences this game will likey fit well in your games library. While there are some things the game could certianly do better I didn't find these issues to detract significantly from the games main draw for me, it's story & premise. I would like to see the game updated with some sort of "Save Game" system that would allow you to "branch off" after each chapter within a single profile. This would make exploring different outcomes easier, howerver, I also can see that this goes against the linear nature of the games concept. The game strives to make you feel like you are participating in the events, that are time bound and as such linear in nature, which have consequences.

Overall I'm enjoying the game and would recommend it to those who enjoy adventure games, visual novels, and mysteries. This isn't really a problem/puzzle solving game (like a "hacker simulator") so if that is what you are looking for you may wish to pass on this game. I definitely recommend it for what it is and I'm really looking forward to the culmination of these events in episode five.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
"The thoughts are free" ... or are they?

Orwell is a pretty neat little game about the potential dangers of openly accessible (or even not so openly accessible) data and the connections and conclusions you can draw from them.

You start out as an investigator for the project "Orwell", a surveillance system meant to protect the people and prevent crimes. 
After a bombing attack you are tasked, together with your supervisor, to find out who was behind the bombings and to prevent further ones.
As you dig deeper through websites and files, desktops and other material, you'll uncover more and more of the story, the motivations of the people responsible for the bombings and uncover some twists and turns throughout your investigations.

The gameplay is pretty simplistic. It's pretty much like surfing through a browser. You can access (predefined) websites and read through articles, blogs and also social media. Throughout the text you find some marked passages, which will help you with your investigation. You can connect these infos with a person and send these infos to Orwell. You can also decide to withhold some informations, letting events turn out differently in the process.

The story and events really sucked me in and were pretty thrilling. Slowly finding out more about the people, their connections to each other, and also be suprised by some twists, made the game very entertaining.

So if you don't mind simplistic gameplay and reading quite a lot and and the topic of data security doesn't turn you down, this is a little gem to keep an eye on.

I'd definitely recommend it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I can't imagine the replayability will be very high, but -- the premise of this game is both great and also very important. Working as a covert tech obtaining info publicly available online in order to put together information on suspects/targets can help shed light on just how much personal information is readily available on almost all people this day and age-- even this review. With due diligence, one can find tons of info on just about anyone. It freaks a lot of people out and seeing a Blue's Clue's version (closest analogy I could think of, game is not much like Blues Clues) might help ameliorate that. A popular tactic of authorities of any sort (hiring managers, law enforcement, parents, whatever) is to comb through someone's social media profile. -- and yet apparently people are still taken aback when someone finds and looks through their facebook profile. 

Anyway... this game addresses a lot of currently important social issues in an engaging and thought-provoking way. It's unique and fun and somehow manages this with being almost entirely text-based.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Great game, I got it in the humble bundle monthly along with other games, and decided to play it because it looked interesting.

Describing the game, it's a very well made point and click adventure, but it's different from your typical point and click games because here you just use Orwell, an operating system designed to watch and monitor people, you can browse different websites and access all sorts of public and private information about your suspects, you go from page to page, phone to phone, computer to computer, device to device, as you try and look for useful information that may help you in your objectives.

The story is short but entertaining and exciting, you get the feeling of really becoming an Orwell 'investigator', the feeling is authentic, the websites, pages, profiles, articles, and that sort of stuff seemed believable enough to get you going into the story. Sometimes the story feels a little bit linear and forced upon you, e.g. pages that you need to look into for information will sometimes be spoonfed to you. but I get it though, if it wasn't though, many people won't know what to do next and get stuck, and they will need to add a lot more useless filler pages/information to make it a more realistic and harder experience. As typical with these kinds of games, there are multiple endings, all affected by your choices in the game. so it adds a bit of replay value.

I only hope they add more episodes/cases next, as the story is a bit short and there is potential for more storytelling using the Orwell system, I also hope they added in voice acting for the voice call tapping parts. so It feels even more authentic. 

I'd also not recommend it for it's full price at the moment(IF they add in more free episodes/cases, then I will change my stance about this, a Season Two is coming though, but that's for another price unfortunately). if you can get it for 50% off, I'd say it's now worth it. For me, I got it in a humble bundle monthly subscription that gives around $200 worth of good games for around $12 a month, along with Rise of the Tomb Raider and other more games.

Score: 7/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] How far are you willing to go to protect the populace? [/h1]

[i]Orwell[/i] is a “visual novel” style game in which you have the ability to follow cyber-breadcrumbs in order to slowly uncover suspect’s online lives. Your goal? Stop a terrorist organization (?) from bombing public spaces. Your tools? As an agent, you are privy to the entirety of your target’s posts, articles, phone calls, emails, etc. Use this information to reveal more and more relevant webpages and conversations. The catch? You’re overlooked by a supervisor and you must choose what information to upload. This supervisor can only see the bits of information you feed him, so choose wisely or risk ruining an innocent’s life. The challenge? Upload only enough information to gain new leads, but not jump to conclusions. 

Are you really helping the greater good by invading the privacy of the few? Or have you caused more harm than good, muddling in affairs you should have never been in? Are the internet spies of today, really the superheroes of tomorrow? Find out by stepping into these large, cyber shoes. Act quickly and stop a harmful event in its tracks, or wait it out and discover it was a false alarm. Big brother is watching you. You are watching the people. Lives are on the line. Decide. 

Then watch as you say, [b]“I never meant for this to happen.”[/b]

Let me start off this review by saying I’m one who really enjoys a story-based game. I particularly enjoy consequence based story games (like [i]Telltale[/i]). If that’s not your cup of tea, this game is not for you. If you’re still interested, here’s the pros and cons for the game so far.

[h1]Pros:[/h1] [b]Interesting social commentary.[/b] There’s no denying that this is the age of technology, and with that comes a whole new slew of problems that our forefathers never could have foresaw when drafting the constitution. [i]Orwell[/i] heavily and obviously alludes to the current hot topics of freedom of internet access, government access to our personal files and correspondences, and general cyber security we see crop up in the news time and time again. 

[b]Easy interface.[/b] There’s not much to learn but drag and drop. Your un-uploaded data chunks are marked so you don’t lose track of what you’ve read, need to read, and are saving for later.

[b]More unique game flow.[/b] Events don’t happen unless you upload data chucks, leaving you to explore the branches of plot in whatever order feels natural to you. It does still feel a bit restricted, though, (see “A bit linear, limited” in cons) a perhaps more of a pseudo-free-directional choice. (But isn’t the concept of freedom what this game is all about?) 

[b]Intriguing artwork.[/b] The geometric artistic style lends itself to unconsciously nod its head towards the cyber-oriented world of the game. It ties in beautifully to the theme of the game—from the logo to the interface—without being too aggressive.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is an incredible 'experience' of a game. Very immersive and gripping story right from the get go.

Characterisation is superbly done, with regular shifts in opinion of characters based on what they may or may not have done, new information comes to light constantly and you as the PC having to delicately manage your personal opinion against what is 'right' and meting out data that will in turn mete out justice.

To some of the other critics here, when looking at the gameplay elements:

There is often frustratingly insufficient evidence to go one way or the other on conflicting information - [i]That's the point[/i]. There's an allegory here for judicial systems of all stripes, that none have perfect information, even here in the information age.
And yes, sometimes you feel the need to submit certain pieces of evidence that aren't in line with the narrative you'd like to create order to progress - [i]That's the point[/i]. I felt conflicted and frustrated as a player of this [i]game[/i]. Imagine the confliction you would have in reality if you knew facts you provide would be wilfully misinterpreted by others to serve their own agenda? To be able to balance such a fine line of generating frustration in a player against the desire to see the story through to conclusion was masterful in my opinion.

A beautiful exploration of this very deep, philosophical point - that is matched by the aesthetic and depth of information to wade through in the game.

Bravo Surprise Attack Games - Orwell sets the bar in this 'cyperpunk storyteller' that will be difficult to surpass; and I'll definitely look forward to the 'datachunk' that you provide.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] George Orwell rolls in his grave [/h1]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is an interactive novel exploring the increasingly popular notion that G. Orwell’s iconic “1984” ended up being a guideline for running a country, rather than a warning to its citizens. True to dystopian tones of its inspiration, the title opens up with a bombing attack on a public plaza. Several people were killed, perpetrators are unknown and public is in an uproar. This where you come in, as hand-picked investigator you will use the latest marvel of civil protection technology – Orwell, to solve the case. Orwell “the first and the last line of defence against terrorism” is a powerful software capable of accessing everything connected to the internet. Once a person is authorised by higher-ups for investigation, you are to upload any useful chunks of data into the software and Orwell will process them, granting you access to further information on the target. Person of interest has their phone number on their social media page? Now you can listen to their calls. An e-mail address published on their company’s website? Let’s take a peek inside. Is that a PC id number? You know the drill by now.

[b] Big brother stays vigilant [/b]
With power of Orwell at your fingertips, the player becomes breach of privacy incarnate, yet the decision whether to upload something or not is yours to make. At times you will have conflicting data, that may mislead the authorities acting upon your investigation, while certain details can be ignored altogether. On the other hand, there are also key data chunks that have to be uploaded in order to progress the story and, especially at early stages, there are not a lot of choices to make. Orwell is counterintuitive at first and software’s interpretation of data provided is downright puzzling at times. You better adapt to your new role quickly, as at certain junctions your choices will have an impact at the rest of the story.

It might have drawn your attention that I have addressed the title in question as an “interactive novel”, rather than a game. This is primarily due to the fact that aforementioned limited choice of data chunks thrown into the system is as far as gameplay goes. Alas, it is much easier to regard Orwell as a book, with webpages being equivalent of descriptions and eavesdropped calls and chats being the dialogues. Your investigation quickly unveils a hint of deeply-rooted conspiracy being at work and bombing is but a beginning of something much bigger. Plot divided into 5 chapters thickens quickly and while the general direction of the story is set in stone, your choices can greatly alter fate of certain characters and the ending is yours to twist.

[b] Blessed be the mind too small to question [/b]
Orwell is rather straight-forward with its thought-provoking intent. While the title’s plot unveils in delightfully ambiguous “The Nation”, it doesn’t take a particularly big leap of logic to start drawing parallels. Especially with themes of invigilation, media manipulation and a classic question of “whether the ends justify the means”. As with most of such questions and ideas, Orwell will be whatever you choose to make of it. It won’t be long though, as the title takes roughly 5 hours to complete, making it possible to finish Orwell in a single sitting. That said, the story is divided into coherent chapters of similar length, highlighted by the game as a good moment for a break, should you need one. Orwell is commendable for finding multiple sensible ways to underline impending conclusion of a plot thread, while staying reasonable from in-universe perspective.

Another facet of Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, deserving a separate mention is the art style of the game. Admittedly, the opening cutscene fells remarkably clunky but everything past this very beginning is static images, allowing the style to truly shine. Every picture is built from colourful polygons giving the illustrations believable, yet somewhat obscured, feel to it. Much like the setting of the story, the visuals are deliberately vague, leaving making the parallels up to the player. 

When approached as a book, Orwell makes for enjoyable read with a highly unorthodox mode of delivery. I can easily recommend it to every fan of criminal thriller and political fiction as you should find yourself right at home. If one were to approach the title as a game though, there is very little to speak of. Should you also happen to be the type to skip dialogues in games as a habit, you should probably avoid Orwell like a plague.

P.S. Once you exit Orwell, you are greeted by advertisement of a sequel - Orwell: Ignorance is Strength. Fear not though, Keeping an Eye On You provides a complete storyline, no “to be continued” ending attached.

review_text_raw:
I've been wanting to write a short but to the point review for this game. Mostly because I rarely finish any games in one go. 

Orwell is [b]NOT[/b] going to WOW you. It's not mindblowing, mind you. It will, however, keep you intrigued once you decide to give it a try. 

[u]What's it about?[/u]

It's heavily influenced by the reveals of Edward Snowden. It's about working in the NSA and uncovering personal data in order to get to the truth. It's about whether or not as people we'd sacrifice our "freedom" or our "safety". Overall, an interesting premise.

[u]Right. It's a game, so what's the gameplay like?[/u]

The "game" consists of reading a lot of text and putting certain bits of it together in order to progress to the next chapters. It doesn't sound too engaging but once you start reading through it, it is able to drag you into its universe. There are multiple endings and choices where you need to choose what to reveal for the people you gather information yourself. 

[u]Multiple choices. Does that mean there's a lot of replayability?[/u]

Well, once you get to the conclusion, you sort of feel fulfilled, hence why many of the reviewers of this game have a few hours of gametime. [b]BUT[/b] I think you can easily play the game a second time to do a few things differently. There is some replayability potential.

Good soundtrack, interesting premise, amusing characters, nice artstyle, engaging storyline. I strongly recommend this game if you want something different.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]Believable writing and gameplay mesh to bring the Orwellian nightmare to life.[/b]

[u][i]Summary:[/i][/u]
With [i]Orwell[/i] literally simulating a job, its success or failure as a game almost entirely hinges on the strength of its writing. Fortunately for all of us, it succeeds with flying colors. The characters it depicts are distinct and memorable. The scenarios it presents to you demand your full attention, else you miss something that leads to catastrophe. In the end it will leave you wondering how else things could have played out.

To be clear, [i]Orwell[/i] is an almost entirely text based experience. It mimics a work computer, including internet browser, email, and even a news and weather report. There is no voice acting, though the voice in my head for each of them is so strong that I had to pause and double check myself on that. Props again to the writers for that. The sound in the game sets a good atmosphere but is limited in quantity to the point of being noticeably repetitive.

If you can stomach the reading load, [i]Orwell[/i] is a novel game that is well worth your time and the cost of admission.

[u][i]Additional details:[/i][/u]
The visual style of [i]Orwell[/i] does an excellent job of being familiar enough to reality while also smoothing over reality's rough edges and mismatching designs. Throughout the game you'll uncover multiple pictures of the same character, often showing different sides of the person than you've seen before. For example you may first discover a finely manicured business photo before later discovering a photo of the same person out on the town, presumably a few drinks in and having a good time. Of course these aren't real photos, but artist renditions.

In order to discuss this next topic, I'll give you the most basic, spoiler free description of what you do in the game. You are tasked with investigating specific people and deciding whether what you find does or does not get added to a government database. Essentially you are both the spy and the filter between your target and the government. With that said, there were a few instances related to this that hampered my immersion. Generally it came from being required to enter a piece of information into the Big Brother system that I would have elected to keep private had it not been needed to progress.

I'll close with a few words on replayability. While there are multiple endings and outcomes to each chapter, I personally didn't feel compelled to replay more than a couple specific moments. The decisions that lead to each result are rarely obvious, so it's hard to go back and change things without reexamining things on a larger scale than I was interested in. There are guides out there that could speed up the process if you're so interested. I happily spent 9 hours with [i]Orwell[/i], nearly all of which was a single careful playthrough.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In [i]Orwell[/i], you are an investigator, employed by a nondescript democratic nation to dig through news, intercepted communications, websites, and personal computers in order to unravel a mystery.

It's not a simulation so much as an interactive story, with several routes to the end, and several possible fates for many of the characters.

Investigate the lives of citizens to find those responsible for a series of terrorist attacks. Your job is solely to go through a heap of modern-day data, everything from standard phone numbers, police files and bank account details, through to more dubious emails, blogs and social media posts. Collecting information, looking for clues, flagging any possible suspects and chasing them down.

You can decide how much of the information you want to sift through as the data chunks are highlighted in blue and easily stand out. There are five episodes in total with each one structured as a ‘day’ and the gameplay will be on average one hour per episode.

A lot of effort went into creating the content for [i]Orwell[/i] and it is really impressive. It’s simple but fun with unexpected twists along the way. Orwell is an excellent experience.

[b]THE GOOD[/b]
- Fascinating Story
- Convincing characters and plot
- Impactful choices and discoveries
- Complex and Innovative
- Fitting soundtrack

[b]THE BAD[/b]
- Text logs of phone conversations feel unnatural

[h1]9/10[/h1]

DISASTER | BAD | MEDIOCRE | OKAY | GOOD | GREAT | [b][u]AMAZING[/u][/b] | MASTERPIECE

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
If I could describe [i]Orwell[/i] in just two words, it would be "surprisingly smart". By that I mean: this is, obviously, a game about ubiquitous government surveillance, and that's not exactly a new theme. It would have been really easy to slap a "Big Brother BAD" plot on this, make it all about how you're one lone hero fighting the implacable government machine, give it a nice feel-good ending and be done with it. Or go the other way and go full grimdark with the boot stamping on a human face, forever. But [i]Orwell[/i] avoids taking the easy way out, and presents a very human story about how real people might act in a world where such a surveillance system exists. Sure, all the endings you can get (and there's a few) are still much more optimistic than George Orwell would be comfortable with, but hey, if you want [i]Nineteen Eighty-Four[/i], you know where to get it.

The gameplay is a simple affair where, in your role as a government agent, you look through available information (websites, chat transcripts, telephone calls) and collect relevant "data chunks", which in turn unlock more avenues for gathering information... and that's less boring than I'm making it sound, honest. For starters, it's not completely linear: sometimes the data you can collect is contradictory, irrelevant, or just plain wrong when taken out of context, and you have to apply your best judgement as to what goes in -- and the very fact that you're telling the system what to think of people based on the information you select comes back to haunt you in the story. Still, if you're looking for a puzzle game, or something that will challenge you beyond "did I forget to click on something somewhere", this isn't it. You're basically here for the story, but there's enough agency that you don't feel like you might as well have been reading a novel.

[i]Orwell[/i] isn't perfect. I got "stuck" once or twice when the game wanted me to put in some information I had deemed not worth uploading, or that I'd left to come back to later when I had more data -- the interface will track what you have and haven't seen, but not what you've seen but haven't acted upon. At these points (and some others) suspension of disbelief suffers a bit by the way the game artificially fences off information that, logically, should be available at any time. The graphics, while suitably stylized, are a bit [i]too[/i] stylized, especially when things need to animate. The music is fine (with some dramatic touches for when you've uncovered particularly dramatic info), but not remarkable. None of these things are deal breakers, though, and overall [i]Orwell[/i] is well worth its price tag as a solid, interactive story experience with an "It Could Happen Here!" theme that makes it that much more compelling.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Lately I've been finding myself bored with many games. I got through the motions without any real investment in what I've been playing... So, I decided to play something different. In comes Orwell. It's unlike any of the games I've toiled mundane hours hacking and slashing away in any random RPGs that I have on rotation. I've been engrossed in it for the past day getting familiar with the intricacies.

This is a different kind of spy game. One that might hit on reality a little closer than I'd like to think. Even more so if I was prone to ideas of the government watching our every move, which is why I'm an active VPN user. But I digress, Orwell is still just a game. A game where you play a data miner looking into the lives of who you might consider dangerous terrorists to a fictitious nation. I should mention there's quite a bit of reading. This isn't your mindless run and shoot game, or hide from the enemies and kill in secret game. It's not even graphically inspiring but the ideas and execution is solid. 

As you're uncovering terrorists and their plots you get deeper into the lives of those you think are involved and have to feed information into the Orwell system to determine their threat level. The game has you scouring through newspapers, blogs, and social media feeds to gain as much information as possible. It would be overwhelming if the interface wasn't so simple to navigate. 

While progression in the game is pretty linear you do have the ability to impact significant events based on what you choose to feed into the system. There is also an abundance of conflicting information that you will have to make judgement calls on what you want to submit. Orwell do a good job highlighting these inconsistencies. The only thing I might have qualms with is there's no "undo" feature. So if you do happen to make a mistake and upload something you'd rather not you don't have a second chance to fix or update your mistakes. The system for all it's abilities has a permanent function. Like most things once it's out there it's there for good. 

In all Orwell is an engaging game where you play big brother and stop terrorists a different way. It's got a solid story and characters and an easy to use interface. It may or may not resemble some truth to life but in the immortal words of Harold Finch "It's not paranoia if they really are out to get you" and in this game you're out to get everyone.

I must say I never heard from that game, after it pops up on Steam at its release date.

And I'm suprised to say, that this game catched me aloen by its name!

I awaited a Big Brother game ... and I got a Big Brother game ... a game, where you can be Big Brother yourself.

You take control of a new surveilance system called Orwell to find the people responsible for a terror bombing.
Fot that you can check websites, 'listen' to calls and chats and search through phones and computers.

Pros:
- Easy to learn gameplay
- Fitting graphic style and background music
- Good story
- 'Just one more minute/level/stage'
- Different endings and outcomes of story parts

Neutral:
- 4-6 hour for a single walkthrough
- Balanced 'Cliché' and 'Suprised' moments/characters

Cons:
- A bit to simple gameplay (there are only some situations, where it is a bit hard to decide between different choices)
- No 'dead ends'
- Linear story progress

As this game offers its first (of five) episodes for free as a demo (works also as a tutorial), you can easily test out, if you like its gameplay. The initial price of around 10 € is very fair, so do the devs a favor if you like the demo and buy it directly. ;)

I really hope the devs use the base concept/gameplay for some more games! I really like that detective style of conecting clues. But at the same time I hope they expend the concept with video footage to analyze, dead ends, more conflicting clues.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I wrote this review after 3 episodes, I might change it later.

Orwell is an interesting game about collecting personal data from people through various means (social media, dating sites, phone calls etc.) and investigating to find the terrorist/s that plant bombs in public places. The gameplay reminds me a lot of Analogue : Hate Story, which is a good sign. Every document gives you new informations, that leads you to new documents etc.

Overall the writing is very solid and believable, you can only see typed messages but they all express the character's personality : the lawyer is writing slowly with perfect punctuation, the young activist uses slang and typos etc. Sometimes there are some blatant shortcuts designed for exposition (a conversation with an unknown person that starts with "What can I do for you, Susan Mills, my best friend from Hugand University ?") but it didn't bother me too much.

What bothers me however is how much the game holds your hand. You can only select a few informations and only about the suspect "du jour". Several times I thought "Wow, Alan is very suspect !" but I couldn't get any informations about him until the next day where I'm told "Today we'll focus on Alan, he's suspect". Am I the investigator or just a goddamn clerk ?

It led to a very aggravating moment where I had to chose between two options, I took the wrong one and innocent people died. To add insult to injury, my sidekick had the nerve to patronize me "What did we do wrong ? If we had taken the other option, this could have been avoided". I think it was meant to emotionally disturb me and make me think that this investigation method is fundamentally flawed, on top of being ethically reprehensible. But instead all I could think was "F*ck you, all informations you ALLOWED me to get pointed at the first option being the good one. You think you're cleverly ambiguous but you're just a cheap mystery novel deliberately misleading the audience to make the plot last long enough".

In conclusion, an extremely lukewarm approval, that might lead to a disapproval if they keep doing this in future episodes. I don't want to replay this game as it feels like Telltale's Walking Dead, where the illusion of choice disappears at the second playthrough where different choices don't impact as much as they seemed.

EDIT : I finished the 5 chapters, I keep my extremely uncommitted approval (lets say 50.1/100).
What limits this game the most is its linearity. I compared it to a mystery novel, it's even worse in late episodes, they want you to suspect specific people in specific orders punctuated by specific twists. You learn in chapter 5 crucial informations that you had no reason not to discover in chapters 1 and 2, since you follow the exact same protocol except the game deliberately kept informations away from you in order to make the game last 5 chapters.

The game also has the nerve to make this railroad look like a social commentary. "You've been chasing the wrong people the entire time, this is the proof that Orwell is unreliable !". Yeah but no, this is just proof that you're putting arbitrary limitations for the sake of the narrative. And even with that, Orwell did better than any other investigation method. Call it unethical, dangerous, tyrannical if you want, but it gets sh*t done and saved lives, and would have done even better without the railroad.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A narrative-driven game, Orwell puts you in the role of a government agent spying on unuspecting citizens' private life in order to maintain peace, law & order. Although, contrary to the inspiration of its namesake, the dystopian world of the videogame doesn't reach the extreme attitudes of "1984" of banned art, love and emotions, but is focused mostly on addressing the issue of abuse of privacy in the name of stability and fighting crime.

In all honesty I hadn't really paid attention in the description and the details of the game and I thought I would have control over a much larger variety of random citizens and decide their fate in unrelated cases, but instead I got involved into a much more story-focused game, sort of a political thriller, where you , the player, much investigate the online presence and phone calls of a group of suspects to decide who is responsible for a series of bombings, with the suspects soon becoming more of a "main/supporting cast" entagled in this one single case . However, my false expecattions didn't hinder my enjoyment of the game as it proved equally fun and interesting.

As for the gameplay, it mostly consists of you reading articles, browsing sites or hacked computers and recorded discussions, uncovering clues that open new places and suspects to investigate but it can feel a little hand-holding especially in the early parts of the game where there is really little to do other than adding all the automatically selected useful information to each suspect's profile and only towards the second half and the end of the game does it provide a little bit more challenge and interesting tougher choices. The outcome can slightly change depending on your actions and the information you provide, although sometimes the game does not exactly make its intentions clear - does it expects you to be good at your job (and the game itself)? Or are you supposed to be a buffoon and ignore vital information about a person's physical and mental health? 
in the second part and especially towards the end of the game where the mechanics shine, it becomes much more interesting and it does a much better job presenting theses questions where the stakes are higher and giving you choices that matter much more and i wish I could see more of this intense decision-making more in the early part.

In terms of graphics i think it's pretty clear that this game will appeal to those who do not need fancy graphics but are fans of endless text boxes. The presenattion is quite good with presenting a dystopian version of the internet and social media,
the artstyle is quite appealing with stylized polygonal semi-realistic pictures and thanks to the story-driven nature of the game, a moody soundtrack that ramps up the intensity when major twists and revelations happen.

review_text_raw: Before buying this game, I saw that most of the top rated reviews just spoke about comparison's to Orwellian works, modern social networks, and Papers Please. And I thought important to address a couple of things after playing through what is available. Orwell is an episodic game; meaning, this is not the final result. This is more of a "Whodunit" than a Thriller mystery, so judging it for linearity might be unfair since they attempt to make you the detective by providing you with a given set of aesthetics. Now talking about aesthetics, this game/experience has its obvious references to Orwell and "1984" -- mainly -- but it is very clear they are only used for inspiration. This is no de facto Orwell Fan Fiction, just an experienced based on some questions the devs had about resembling aspects of society. From the two episodes they have released, I can tell that this is comparable to Papers Please in that you have to provide an analysis to come up with game altering decisions. However, since this is a "Whodunit" type mystery, and are limited to less than half of the intended story arc, we cannot truly make that comparison. What I can say without spoiling, is that there are choices that can either save or spare hundreds of lives, and the deciding factor is actually a juxtaposition of logic I have yet to fully grasp and understand. I think this is a great game; yet, it remains an aesthetic experience we are not yet able to finalise. I look forward for Episode 3's release in three day's time.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
8/10 Very Good.

Every once in a while, a game will come along that you simply won’t put down and will try to finish in one sitting. For me, Orwell fits that category, for it was thoroughly engrossing.

As the name suggests, Orwell deals with privacy and government surveillance. You are an ‘investigator’ of the new Orwell application, an app which, with the right authorisation, allows you to snoop on people’s phone calls, e-mails and all their online histories at will.

It is a disturbing look into a surveillance state, and yet, by putting you in charge it opens the door (and your mind) to justifying the system.

In the introduction, there is a terrorist bombing that kills some people. That’s where you come in, you’re in to investigate the prime suspect and ultimately to bring down the terror cell. You pick datachunks, which is vital (and non-vital/misleading) information and assign it to a person of interest in order to shape a narrative about them.

For example, you can use it properly in order to keep the authorities informed about a person’s whereabouts or connections with other people. Likewise, you can misuse it, say you might see a Twitter conversation where someone says “oh that’s torture!” (in reference to being taken out nightclubbing to dance) and the system will update to suggest that the person in question is, actually, a genuine torturer.

It is pretty obvious that Orwell intends for you to use your best judgement in the situation, take it seriously as a proper investigative tool and suddenly the arguments for invasive surveillance look quite appealing, especially if you succeed in foiling terror actions. Use it inappropriately on the other hand and suddenly things look a bit bleak.

For me, Orwell’s story was enticing and gripping. I was captivated trying to deny the terror actions, but also by the investigation into the terror cell. I don’t want to spoil anything, but basically, I swept through this in one sitting, without breaks, in just over four hours.

Why not a higher score? Well, I did encounter some bugs. At one point in a new chapter it would keep defaulting back to the previous chapter’s screens. I had to reboot the game in order to cut this nonsense out and continue. Without these, I may very well have given a 9, but I think that perhaps, would be too generous given the nature of the game. Still, this is a very good game.

review_text_raw:
Duration: Just under 5 hours. 

Orwell is a very unique game.  The player takes the persona of an investigator in a futuristic 1984-style society and tries to find information/evidence regarding some terrorist bombings.  There are 5 chapters in the game which take you on a journey.  The first chapter you are closely led by your examiner, but then more and more choices are laid before you as you delve into websites, eavesdrop on phone calls and investigate hard drives.  

The game is somewhat linear and the main choice is to choose if information is relevant or not to the case and avoiding taking things out of context.  For once you claim something is true, it is stuck in stone.  

Overall, playing Orwell (after the first 60 minutes) became a highly engrossing experience.  The delivery is very well done and even builds to a massive tension where getting information at one point is almost frantic as you are listening to a phone call.  I won't give the details away, but it was tense and somewhat chilling conclusion.  

Overall, a very unique game, full of reading text, but well-delivered. 

7/10 Recommended.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] An Excellent Educational Tool for Teaching People the Value of Privacy [/h1]

I am going to start this review with a hot take: people don't care much about privacy. At least not in the way we're taught to think about it. People desire privacy when they want to hide from others—especially people they know. A classic example of this is your average teenager concealing their sexual activity from their parents. We can define this as [b]interpersonal privacy[/b]—the need and right to keep parts of ourselves hidden from the people around us. In a limited sense, people do care about having (intepersonal) privacy  in their lives. 

But what about a faceless entity like a government agency or a big tech company? Should we seek privacy from their probing eyes? Do we even deserve the right to privacy from the government and Big Tech? This is precisely where people will shrug their shoulders and say that they don't understand or care. Interpersonal privacy matters to the common man. Privacy from institutions and systems does not.

Why are we like this? The reasons for this range from the righteous to the fearful to the misguided.

[list]
[*] Fear: A citizen concerned for their safety will give up essential liberty as Ben Franklin pointed out. This was evident after the Patriot Act was passed. It was evident again after the Snowden leaks. People feel like they will be safe from violent crime if they give up rights. As Franklin rightly noted, this safety is but temporary. It is futile to give up your rights to secure it.
[*] Righteousness: Many people use the 'nothing to hide' fallacy to justify the lack of privacy. People will say that they are not criminals. And so, they have nothing to hide from the government. This righteousness is misguided because it is based on the presumption that governments are always righteous and have the best intentions for their subjects. Governments can and do turn tyrannical—when they do, they spy on and punish citizens.
[*] Ignorance (of consequence): People do not understand how much private information the government and BIg Tech has about them. Information is power—this is especially true in the age of data. Information about you can be used to easily understand and manipulate you. But people do not understand how private information is collected and misused. And so they don't care about privacy. [/list]

Educating people about the need for, let alone the right to privacy is a challenging task. We need to reframe and redirect the conversation away from interpersonal privacy to privacy from insitutions. Doing this is difficult because institutional surveillance feels like an abstract concept to many. This is precisely where the game Orwell excels. Osmotic Studios does a great job of showing why your life should be private from the government and Big Tech. In Orwell, you play as a government agent snooping on ordinary citizens. You gather personal information for a surveillance system designed to store data and weaponize it. Every piece of information you harvest is used to create damaging narratives, justify injustice and enable tyranny. The net result of your gameplay is acutely felt on a personal level. Your actions lead to individuals being maligned, families torn apart and the world becoming worse.

Orwell is thus a great educational tool for privacy advocates looking to teach the public about the value of and the right to privacy.

[h1] Recommendations for Specific Gamers [/h1]

[h2] Voyeuristic & Paranoid Gamers [/h2]
[list]
[*] Do you lie in bed with your partner, look at him and think to yourself: "I bet he's thinking about other women."
[*] Do you spy on your loving girlfriend's phone because you constantly suspect her of using dating apps?
[*] Are you a chai enthusiast who loves to talk about tea with other women on Tea apps?
[*] Or perhaps you are a masculine married man who revels in the simple joys of candaulism?
[/list]

If you answered yes to any of these questions, you must play Orwell! The game is a voyeur's delight. It will scratch every voyeuristic itch—and trust issues—that you have.

[h2] Gamers Who Love to Gaslight & Manipulate [/h2]
Orwell not only allows you to spy on people but also to shape the narrative about them. Do you want a woman to be seen as a loving single mom who dotes on her child? Or do you want her to be seen as a mentally unstable terrorist who commits violence? You have the power to choose in Orwell! 

This ability to manipulate and shape narratives is one of the best gameplay mechanics in Orwell. You can gaslight the government itself into believing what you want them to believe! Wonderful! This is exactly why video games appeal to the male fantasy!

Bottom line:  I cared too much about getting things right while playing Orwell. But the game doesn't want you to do that! In fact, creating a false narrative about NPC characters is required for some achievements. So yeah, don't worry too much. Go ahead and play fast and loose with the truth!

[h2] 1984 Enjoyers [/h2]
Let's get this straight: Orwell is a great tool to teach people about privacy. But it is no literary masterpeice. Yes the game pays homage to 1984. But Orwell treads familiar ground about liberty, security and privacy. It is not designed to be a sophisticated commentary on the issues and concepts it deals with.

That said, I loved the character of Abraham Goldfels. He is a fascinating case study of a person who is co-opted by the very surveillance state he is trying to fight. Abraham is a complicated character with ambiguous motivations. I started the game feeling a sense of admiration for his intellectual nature and ability to lead. I ended the game feeling conflicted about his past and his life choices. What do you think of Abraham? Leave a message in the comments sections if you'd like to talk about him!

[h2] Reading Haters [/h2]
Orwell is a text heavy game. You will be reading and analyzing articles, chat logs, documents, emails and much more. For those who love reading books, Orwell is an enjoyable game. But those who dislike reading will struggle.

My eyes did sometimes glaze over the many walls of text I went through. Fortuntately, the plot and gameplay is engaging enough to sustain you through. The first episode feels sluggish as you learn the ropes of the game. But keep at it: Orwell gets a lot more interesting in the later acts.

[h2] Atmospheric Music Enjoyers [/h2]
Orwell's soundtrack is definitely vibey. The slow and atmospheric music gets you in the mood of being a detective who is investigating criminal cases. Not a music critic so I can't say more than that.

[h2] Achievement/Completionist Hunters [/h2]
The game is not too hard for achievement hunters and completionists. Multiple playthroughs are not needed. You only need to replay some episodes to get specific achievements. I recommend [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=907778579] using this achievement guide [/url] which helped me get 100%.

Warning: Orwell is buggy and suffers from major save file issues. Backing up game files will not help IMO because of the persistent autosave feature. The first time I played Orwell, I lost progress and so I quit playing. The second time around, I finished the game and then bounced between chapters to get the remaining achievements. Once again, the game tripped up and asked me to replay the game from scratch!

My advice is to play through the game once. Then check which achievements you need and which episodes they fall in. Need achievements for Episodes 4 & 5? Replay [b] those episodes first in chronological order [/b]. If necessary, repeat the episodes until you get all the episode specific achievements.

For Episodes 1-3, I recommend creating a [b] separate profile [/b] and then playing the episodes in order. Episode 3 in particular is a mess because you have to replay it 3 times at least to get the achievements! 

[h1] Overall Rating [/h1]
[b] WIP, FIS, IIS
2+2=5/6 [/b]

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The true strength of Orwell lies not in replayability, or even in a strong gameplay mechanic, but in a consuming immersion that relays a story illustrating how powerful a government powered by surveillance could truly be.  You "live" what it would really mean to the lives of people you begin to learn more and about as you coldly monitor them in what feels like real time. 

Unlike other games employing immersive story driven simulations on rails, like "This is the Police" or Uplink, I never once sought to find a "right" solution online.  I accepted that my data was only as good as the research I could see in front of me, and I made some calls based on the psychology of the subjects I digitally (legally) stalked, for the good of The Nation.  By the middle of the game, I couldn't really stop.  It was like binging Netflix, and although pulling back I can clearly see that the game is often holding your hand and guiding you towards the next arc, in the moment the progression feels so natural that I was just excited to unravel the next thread. I performed my role in the Orwell program compliantly. 

The music and the Minority Report style slick UI (that felt so good to work in), combined with the friendly banter of your friendly government advisor led me to the worst part about this game - I started it at 11pm.  I had work at 8am the next day, which only allowed a couple hours of sleep after finally beating the game over 6 straight hours.  

There are unique endings, and the game will bend based on your choices and how far you dig.  When investigating, you don't have to read deeply into every article - Orwell finds the pertinent data for you so you're not forced to muddle through what turns into a mountain of documentation.  Sometimes though, you really need to step back and figure out your suspects murder mystery style, except you do it by going through their files, emails, phone call transcripts, timelines, and chat logs - tying that in with publically available resources. 

And maybe that's the biggest lesson of the game, and of 1984 when you apply a technical layer - in a society where we are constantly generating documents and digital paper trails, you could really learn all you need to know to paint us as however you'd like with the right tools.  It's one thing to read it, but the game lets you feel it. All at once it was exciting, and chilling.

In the end, without offering spoilers, the game never forces you to choose if this is right or wrong.

The total time to beat the game, for me, was 5 hours, but hardly any of that was spent idle. For $10 (I got this on sale at $6), if you have even half the experience I did, the game proves its value quickly.  While you can only replay the game the same way you would reread a book (altered maybe slightly), it did give me a short story worth thinking about for much longer than the gameplay itself lasted.


Pros:

- Immersive gameplay and story
- Great soundtrack
- UI feels fantastic
- Great value
- Story ending felt wrapped up, not abrupt

Cons:

- Limited replayability
- 5 hours of content (I take the time to read a lot of the docs)
- Not super challenging to an average player

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
You know all those safety measures we usually take (or fail to take online) for fear our personal info may be compromised and exploited by the powers that be? Well, Orwell puts you in the shoes of one of those people who collect such data. An outsourced data processor hired by the government.
Most of the time you will be selecting data chunks and uploading them to the mainframe of a huge, centralised surveillance hub. This explains both the concept and the mechanics of the game. The game is not linear and the story branches depending on your choices.

The story is fairly engaging, but the questions and dilemmas that the game deals with are even more compelling. If you are interested in the matters of online privacy, online identity, laws on privacy, data collecting engines or even just dystopia in general, this is a game for you.

That said, the game has its shortcomings in that the story, when you find out all the bits, does not really always add up in the most logical of ways, particularly if you choose some of the more exotic routes of the story.

Still, the experience itself is fairly novel, so this one gets an unreserved recommendation.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What would you do if you really wanted to imprison some people that irked you? Obviously, you would scour their Facebook, Twitter, and eHarmony profiles to gather evidence of corroboration between them and terrorist activist cells. Atleast that’s how Osmotic Studios would do it. Although it may be a bit of a crude hyperbole, that is essentially what you will be doing in Orwell, the fascinating game where you play as Big Brother in an effort to keep The Nation safe and discover the culprits behind the recent bombing events in the capital city.

[h1]Privacy vs Security[/h1]

Other than being the author of 1984, the story where this game gets many of its motifs from, Orwell is rebirthed as a new governmental security program created to maintain order and reduce crime in a totalitarian country called, The Nation. Being an all-encompassing program with no bounds in breaking personal privacy, Orwell has the ability to retrieve: medical records, user submitted online information, bank statements, school records, mobile device data, telephone calls, chat room conversations, and pc device data. Your role in ensuring the safety of The Nation is in the capacity of an investigator, one who has authority to utilize the Orwell mainframe as an unbiased outsider to The Nation. As an investigator, you must sift through all of the information Orwell retrieves to discover and submit “relevant” datachunks to your immediate supervisor. What you deem relevant will shape the futures of the suspects under investigation, so take great care in deciding what to submit to Orwell.

Gameplay-wise, Orwell’s UI behaves much like an internet browser with three major utilities: the Reader, Listener, and Insider. These utilities allow you to pull up internet-related articles, tap into phone calls or chat conversations, or remote control mobile/PC devices respectively. Throughout the countless scripts of text provided by the articles or conversations, datachunks are automatically highlighted, and notifications beside specific entries where datachunks are present help guide the player towards progression. Some datachunks will be relatively useless, such as a person’s favorite color, but others will be extremely relevant to the case. Chunk by chunk, you will eventually develop fully-fleshed profiles to aid you in determining who the next person of interest is until the final culprit is found.

[h1]License to Know[/h1]

Using Orwell's features is the crux of the game, letting you slowly form your own opinion on who may be innocent or an accomplice, all while unraveling deeper motivations about the suspects and influential figures around you and Orwell. When you think you've cleanly profiled someone, post-incident reports will reveal multiple perspectives with conflicting beliefs that you may have never even thought of. As each episode focuses on a different character, everyone feels really well developed and sharply defined by disparate personalities and lifestyles. In addition, the more you learn about one thing, the less confident you will feel about another. 

Although the detective aspect of the game begins off strong, it unfortunately slowly undermines itself due to the fact that every clue is essentially hand-fed to the player. Since notifications of datachunks are provided, what ended up seeming to be a neat and helpful feature to ensure that I can progress without too much trouble began to feel like a massive crutch. This created an extremely casual playstyle where I was really just along for the ride. Don't get me wrong, it is still one great journey, but the immersiveness could have been kicked up a notch by providing players a serious investigative challenge. For example, if all notifications and highlighted entries were removed, it would definitely force me to care much more about the seemingly mundane or extraneous text for fear of relevancy. Finding the clues could be as "simple" as manually highlighting useful data. The supervisor continued to nag me about looking for X, finding X, learning more about X, but eventually the clues led me there without trying anyways. I felt like I might as well just speed-read anything without highlighted text in it to quickly move on. 

In addition, certain clues must be fed to Orwell to proceed, even if I wanted to exclude it. The game seems to make a big deal about being careful what to upload to the mainframe, so why force me to make choices like that. Maybe I'm inclined to believe X is innocent, but to proceed, I must upload information that X has a military background in order to create clearance for investigation. Having this feature further supports the casual mindset of submitting anything that is highlighted and diminishes the need to read everything or even care. Don’t get me wrong, the game still provides the players with a fair amount of control, since the endings are vastly different and minor paths will affect the outcome of certain suspects, but I definitely did not welcome the need to have milestone/checkpoint datachunks for progression.

The datachunk system still has some pretty neat features though, most notably in regards to data conflicts. At these moments, two conflicting statements are uncovered and only one can be submitted. You will essentially provide info that you want your supervisor to act upon. Ex. "I heard X was home last night....[phone conversation]" vs "Me and X had a blast at the concert last night [social networking site]." What you choose will relatively dictate what will happen to X. These conflicts returned a little bit of control taken away with the abovementioned checkpoint chunks.

[h1]Complete Walkthrough Playlist[/h1]

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s6Q75R9yWtU&list=PLeavCsRFiP55ATTks7hLjJY84dnSIXY3y&index=1

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

At first, Orwell seemed to have been just a more interactive visual novel or point & click game, but certain scripted scenes suddenly thrust me into Orwell's world, making me experience the exact same feelings a tech-savvy security investigator would be facing. Times where I would suddenly lose access to Orwell's mainframe, experience a cyber-attack, discover life-threatening secrets or aid Orwell during an active escape attempt. I found myself making motions and exasperations my virtual counterpart would most likely make, and the intense emotions I felt during these moments are something that would be highly difficult to forget as I walk away from the game. I can't recall any visual novels or point & clicks that have made me feel so involved in its world, seemingly shaping the final conclusion to the story.

Even though I have some gripes with Orwell’s progression and datachunk systems, the game is a far cry from being a failure at its attempt to tell a captivating story with novel methods. It isn’t easy for a game to present information in such a way to draw strong opinions from the players, yet manage to continually make their beliefs sway back and forth. The developers, however, knew how to create false trails, dead ends, probable causes and multiple motivations yet skew them towards a believable conclusion. Furthermore, scripted moments that nearly broke the fourth wall created a unique sense of immersion and relatability. This makes it very easy for me to recommend Orwell to any fan of story-centric narratives or spy games. If you’re still on the fence about this game, try the demo. It is free and contains the entire first episode - and it only gets better from there.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The premise is simple:
It's a game where you play a investigator who works for the government, sifting through data in all of its forms in order to fight for the safety of the public in the fictional world that it's set in.

There have been many 'hacking' games that have come out over the years, but Orwell takes the idea and puts you in the position of 'good' rather than 'bad', which creates the core ideology of the game -- If what you're doing is so good, then why do you feel so bad doing it?

The game proceeds along a UI of sorts, one that allows you to sift through websites, personal pages and even listen on some incredibly well-simulated 'real time chats', along with interruptions and intentional spelling errors that betray the typer's emotions and mental states. It's one of the best simulations of texting I've seen before in a game, and it DOES stand out. The articles and websites, while simple and clean, are detailed and packed full of worldbuilding -- the developers go out of their way to fill the world with detail that was never necessary to get from point A to B, but still fill everything with life and activity, and the world ends up feeling a little bit less compartmentalized than other games which force you into a limited POV.

However, this all leads back to the internal condundrum I have with this game:
You work with a handler who analyses the information you send him, and it's his job to make sense of it all. All you do is forward him the pertinent information, enough for him to make decisions and calls on how to handle situations. And you must choose what it is you want to send.

It's your choice to pick A over B. And it's not outright lies, because you're the good guy, remember? But whatever you send can tinge a thought, affect outcomes and colour perceptions in slight, yet pertinent, ways. Your own analysis plays a big part in how you want to portray someone else, and ultimately, the only one who has to live with the decisions you make is yourself.

Orwell is a great game about people, but more than that, it's a platform to help you examine yourself as a person. Since you're doing this for the percieved good, what decisions will you make and how far will you go to get what you want? And is there ever a time when personal freedom can be infringed upon for the greater result? Well... that might be another question for another time.

It's a good game tho, eh?

(( P.S.: Like any other 'visual novel' style game, and including the horrendous works of Mr. David Cage, I am fully aware that some of these 'choices' may be nothing more than illusionary. However, the game does it well enough in its context that reflecting upon the choices you make actually makes more than just a surface-level difference since you're playing not a character, but yourself. And considering the game's name and influences, I believe this to be the point. ))

review_text_raw:
[b]TL:DR: [/b] Does 1984 ring a bell? Yes? You are all good, skip this. No? Block off four hours and prepare a lighthearted movie after to flush the existential horror.

[h1]What is Orwell?[/h1]
The player takes the role of an independent third party taking the reigns of the most powerful surveillance technology ever built tasked with the investigation of a terrorist attack on a monument in the capital of a fictitious country called The Nation. Armed with a context sensitive browser the player dives head first into one medium deep rabbit hole.

[h1]Game Design | The Awesome (+2)[/h1]
I adore the brutalist functionality of the game design. It feels like a desk job. There is nothing special to it. Everything works as one would expect it to. It should feel cold. It should provide a degree of separation from the subject while not hindering gameplay. This is one of the hardest tricks any game designer can pull off. Take it from a boring person who unironically loves to create spreadsheets for any number of things. This [i]rocks[/i].

[h1]Audio design | The Terrible (-2)[/h1]
Coming in on the opposite side of the spectrum is audio design. Or lack thereof. The only notable attempt at anything are dynamic music changes when the player comes across [i]shocking[/i] new information. And yes, I am exaggerating, because the music is exaggerating. The whiplash from the norm is that great. It arrives suddenly and leaves before it had a chance to order a frickin' latte. Then there are all the missed opportunities. The player has access to various types of data from texts, to web pages, to voice calls. Instead of a transcript it would have been great to have the few calls fully voiced. It would have brought the player even closer to the characters.

...of which Orwell utilizes several one dimensional archetypes with a couple of exceptions that show a hint of a second dimension. Fortunately for the game, the player is not forced to linger on any of the cast. We get just as much as we need to understand from where the wind is blowing before moving on to the next person. For better or worse, commentary on surveillance killing the human experience acts as the main character of the game and is largely responsible for the ankle deep depth of the human pawns.

[h1]Closing Thoughts | The Adequate (0)[/h1]
Orwell is a tricky proposition. On one side it is concise, excellently showcases pitfalls of absolute surveillance and should be a mandatory play on any high school, on the other side it is cynical to the core and does not allow a solution of the privacy/security conundrum. I could speculate that the original intention of the authors was to show the only winning move is not to play. However, I am writing this script seven years after the release in a world that is inching closer and closer to a world of AI driven absolute surveillance. The absolute surveillance of Orwell fails even with a human at the helm of its moral compass, what chance do we have in the real world without such an agent? At the end of the day art is a reflection of our perceived reality. I understand that having no way out nets a more chilling experience. However, if the resolution does not provide a positive outlook, something to aspire to, it leaves the observer in a very dark place.

review_text_raw:
Intro:

 Eric Arthur Blair (famously known under the pen name of George Orwell) was a essayist (someone who writes essays for a living), novelist, critic and journalist.  He lived between 25th of June 1903 to 21th of January 1950 and was most famous for two books.  Namely Animal Farm (17 August 1945) and 1984 (8 June 1949).  Animal Farm is considered to be a classic of allegorical story-telling and political satire. 1984 on the other hand is a book where endless parallels can be drawn to in real life. 

Where the grim (sometimes terrifying) warnings of totalitarianism, twisting of words, meaning and history appear to become more of an reality.  1984 is considered to be one of the best books ever written (an opinion that I share myself).  Its influence on narrative art, politics and language cannot be understated.  Today’s game: Orwell owes a lot to 1984, right down to naming itself after Blair’s pen surname.  

Story:

One of the game’s themes and commentary is how people present themselves online and “offline”.  This is no more evident than with the various interactions the small groups of characters have with each other.  Cassandra Watergate (get it?!) is on one hand,  an emotionally unstable, childish woman who  does not care about adult responsibility.  However on the other hand she is apparently a activist who might have been responsible for a series of bombings and assaults on police. 

Which character is the real thing? That is what helps make the story compelling, Orwell sets up characters that behave in unique ways, behaviour patterns that often conflict with your perception and then ask you to decide who they are.  People are very different online and in the presence of other people (could this man be impersonating another man who might not even be alive?!).  Orwell uses limited perception and distorted character presentation to compel the player to continue playing. 

Gameplay:

Gameplay is rather easy and straightforward.  You use Orwell to find data on various persons supposedly involved in terrorist activities. In order to uncover who was responsible and who was not. Relevant information is highlighted in blue.  At worst you have to decide which information is relevant to which character.  You would also have to decide what information is important or valid (someone saying that they are from wonderland is not valid for obvious reasons).  However there is not much of a failure (at least for me )  as all I got was a scolding from Symes.  However I did find myself debating on the various behaviour patterns and deciding which behaviour fits with the character’s overall personality. Orwell might be easy but that does not mean it is not compelling.  Simple but straightforward and very polished. 

Conclusion:

Orwell’s relevance is undeniable, the balance between private and public with the invention of Social media has become.  The encroachment of government surveillance for safety from a threat that might not exist is a legitimate possibility.  The erasure of privacy encouraged by the likes of Facebook and Twitter. Where everything you say and do is recorded to be sold to the highest bidder.  Orwell’s importance as a game will always be relevant while Britain and China’s surveillance states continue to become more of a reality.
